title: The Truth About Greatness ft. Mike & Paul Rabil, Founders of the Premier Lacrosse League
guest: Mike Rabil (CEO) and Paul Rabil (President and lacrosse legend), co-founders of the Premier Lacrosse League
summary: Brothers Mike and Paul Rabil explain how they rebranded professional lacrosse into the PLL using a wholly-owned, tour-based model, why sports leagues need duration rather than tech-style escape velocity, and why sports is defensible against AI. The conversation turns into sibling co-founder 'therapy' as both duos discuss rivalry, lanes of ownership, imposter syndrome, and a real fight the Tiger Sisters had over a missed email.

ideas.idea: The PLL didn't invent a sport; it rebranded and reintroduced professional lacrosse because the existing league wasn't serving players and fans in a modern tech and media environment.
ideas.detail: Lacrosse has been played in North America for thousands of years, in college since the 1800s, and was in the early-1900s Olympics; it returns in the 2028 Olympics. The PLL just finished its seventh season and launches the women's league (WLL) with four inaugural teams next year.

ideas.idea: A co-founder with a different brain is essential, and being brothers is what kept the company alive through clashes because they refuse to give up on each other.
ideas.detail: Mike says if Paul weren't his brother he probably would have quit after too many co-founder clashes. Growing up, 22 months apart, they had a rule to always play on the same team in pickup sports because opposite teams ended in fist fights.

ideas.idea: A sports league can't push its launch date like a tech startup because 200 players, ticket buyers, venues and a network are all counting on a fixed date.
ideas.detail: Paul contrasts event businesses with technology startups; the PLL launch was a dramatic series of moments to execute from 'good idea' to the start line.

ideas.idea: A wholly-owned, tour-based league model gives economies of scale on costs and full IP ownership, letting you package sponsor and media-rights deals quickly and scale revenue nationally.
ideas.detail: The next evolution is bringing in local team owners who invest 365 days a year and build real estate around teams, because sports are communal and hyperlocal and that's what the national model was missing.

ideas.idea: Sports leagues need duration, not tech-style escape velocity; you pound the rock with consistent growth until a superstar or moment arrives.
ideas.detail: Venture LPs ask 'seven seasons, what's up?' but the NBA was tape-delayed and losing money in the early 80s until Jordan, Bird and Magic; the WNBA got Caitlin Clark. The PLL has long-term investors and early superstars, and is growing every year.

ideas.idea: Sports is the last great unifier and arguably America's last great export and lever for global influence.
ideas.detail: Cherie attributes the 'last great export' framing to PLL investor Joe Tsai; sports is one of the last things that brings people together in person.

ideas.idea: Sports is more defensible to AI than any other industry because you can't prompt a physical skill and fans need human error.
ideas.detail: A robot hitting 100 threes in a row would go viral once and then nobody would watch; Jordan's dunks matter because another player feels pain. AI perfects human error elsewhere, sports requires it.

ideas.idea: Sports is a great advertising business because it reliably elicits an uncertain feeling (anticipation then payoff or letdown) that every brand wants to attach itself to.
ideas.detail: Human beings are driven by feelings, and sports is one of the few products that delivers that state with surety, so brands buy placement next to it.

ideas.idea: When competing for attention, don't service what you think fans want; build content, production and rules that entertain you, and bet that obsessed authenticity attracts others.
ideas.detail: Paul references Rick Rubin's 'The Creative Act' on the hosts' shelf and applies it to their podcast: have a unique point of view, be consistent, and enjoy the show you make. The PLL wants to be a top-five team sports league but may not get there in their lifetime for reasons outside their control.

ideas.idea: You can't force people to watch, but you can condition fans the way the NBA and NFL did by teaching them how to show up, attend and build rituals.
ideas.detail: Many lacrosse fans grew up watching the college game but never paid for a pro ticket; David Stern and Adam Silver conditioned NBA fans in the 80s and 90s, and NFL tailgating four hours before kickoff was created. The PLL does this while simultaneously building infrastructure.

ideas.idea: Strength and speed get you out of the gate, but endurance over time, rooted in authentic passion, is what wins in sports, podcasts and the creator economy.
ideas.detail: 'Strength, speed and endurance' becomes the episode's motto; the hosts plan to make a carousel of it.

ideas.idea: Imposter syndrome is healthy and is what drives most top athletes and entertainers, but you should check whether it comes from 'not enough' or insatiable desire, both of which are vices.
ideas.detail: Coaches wove it into sports culture ('they're better than us, this is a trap game'); the imaginary rival in West Texas working harder gives you the last rep. Paul carried the judgment of being paid $15,000 at the top of pro lacrosse while NBA/NFL/MLB peers got rewarded, and that followed him into business rooms.

ideas.idea: Women athletes have a faster and better path to becoming superstars, so building a platform around today's women's lacrosse stars makes business sense.
ideas.detail: Credit goes to 30 years of the WNBA and three iterations of pro women's soccer; women have always been featured more in advertising, are more empathetic and have more diverse interests reaching broader audiences.

ideas.idea: Co-founders avoid blow-ups by respecting each other's lanes of ownership and horsepower rather than overlapping on the same work.
ideas.detail: Mike sees tech co-founder blow-ups when both are engineers or both are business people arguing over the same thing while another area of the room goes uncleaned. Big decisions are made together, but each owns their area.

ideas.idea: Disagreements at an impasse can't always be solved logically, so revert to empathy and trade concessions ('you take this one, I'll take the next').
ideas.detail: Both brothers arrive with strong, well-researched positions; Paul is 'relentless' and more likely to bend rules to win. Conflict shouldn't be constant but you need friction to run fast, like a foot hitting the ground.

ideas.idea: The Tiger Sisters think they should disagree more, because their similar training makes them too aligned and more conflict would produce 10x crazier ideas.
ideas.detail: Cherie copied Jean's career (both elite business school and tech) and pushed Jean into a CS degree so no engineer could question her as a PM; Jean went straight into an APM role from undergrad as one of four LinkedIn interns. Now they're adjusting from second-parent/younger-child to peers and co-founders.

ideas.idea: Working with a sibling shortcuts professionalism and triggers parent-child and birth-order dynamics, so feedback lands as an attack even when it comes from care.
ideas.detail: After Jean missed a red-lines email on the biggest brand deal ever (10x any prior deal), Cherie's 'put me on the email' implied she wouldn't have missed it and felt like parenting from the younger sister. Paul notes 40 years of sibling history is 'psychological warfare' baked in; Mike says a non-sibling partner would have led with empathy first.

ideas.idea: When you feel yourself getting hot, pull out, breathe and respond afterward; and if you react anyway, apologize fast because apologies cost nothing and mean a lot.
ideas.detail: Mike lets his body signal when he's hot and adjusts; Cherie apologized within five minutes. Missing one email over a working weekend doesn't kill a deal and following up shows you care.

ideas.idea: Family businesses that make it get undying loyalty, commitment and respect that you'll never find in a non-sibling partner.
ideas.detail: The ingrained rivalry is why many families don't go into business together, but for those who do, no one is as committed as a sibling.
